title: Power Pages: client APIs for scripting forms, lists, users and data
summary: The roadmap details, control paths, deployment commands and carefully qualified licensing statements are supported. Minor corrections should acknowledge Microsoft's separate anonymous-access governance guidance and add the cloud-flow web-role control to the table.

claims.where: front matter: licensing.notes; Cost and licensing
claims.claim: Power Pages capacity licensing measures authenticated and anonymous users per website per month.
claims.quote: Power Pages (formerly Power Apps portals) licensing is capacity based and offers two types of capacities based on user type: Authenticated users per website/month and Anonymous users per website/month.

claims.claim: Portals Web API operations require a Power Pages licence.
claims.quote: Portals Web API operations require a Power Pages license.

claims.claim: Anonymous portals Web API calls count towards anonymous user capacity.
claims.quote: Web API calls made by anonymous users count towards the anonymous user capacity.

claims.claim: Authenticated portals Web API callers require applicable authenticated user capacity licences.
claims.quote: Web API calls made by authenticated users (internal or external) don't count towards page views, but require applicable authenticated user capacity licenses.

claims.claim: Learn does not explicitly explain whether client API calls have different capacity treatment or inherit portals Web API licensing unchanged.
claims.quote: Searched: Power Pages "$pages.webAPI" "Webapi" settings licensing capacity; "Power Pages" "client API" "license". Read client-api/dataverse, ajax, web-api-overview and Power Pages licensing FAQ passages; no client API-specific capacity treatment.

claims.claim: Power Pages cloud flow integration requires a Power Automate licence.

claims.claim: Microsoft recommends a Power Automate Process licence for production cloud flow integration.
claims.quote: It's recommended to use a Power Automate Process license in the production instance.

claims.quote: Searched: "Power Pages" "client API" "license". Opened client-api/agents in full; it documents SendActivity, callbacks, examples and errors, with no licensing section or requirement.

claims.where: summary; Why it matters; Risk assessment; controls[0].note; rationale: risk
claims.claim: Power Pages enforces table permissions on the server and the client API cannot override them.
claims.quote: Power Pages applies form metadata and table permissions on the server, and the client API can't override those settings.

claims.where: Risk assessment: Data exposure; Governance guidance
claims.claim: Granting the Anonymous users web role table access makes the table's data available to any visitor.
claims.quote: When the Anonymous users web role is granted access to a table, any user who visits the site can access the data in the table.
claims.fix: Retain the cited warning, but also cite https://learn.microsoft.com/power-pages/security/disable-anonymous-access and explain its qualification: the tenant's Anonymous access to Dataverse control can block anonymous reads despite maker table permissions; anonymous writes can remain possible. That separate Microsoft page says the control overrides maker configurations.

claims.where: Risk assessment: Data exposure; Governance guidance
claims.claim: setVisible(false) hides controls only in the browser, not as a security boundary.
claims.quote: The setVisible(false) method hides a control in the browser only. Use table permissions and column security to protect data. Never rely on hiding a control to secure data.

claims.claim: Hiding a list row changes presentation rather than server-returned data.
claims.quote: Hiding a row changes only what people see in the list; it doesn't change the data or the number of records that the server returns.

claims.claim: Changing a control's disabled state is not a way to override server-side restrictions.
claims.quote: When a control is locked on the server, such as a multiselect picklist on a read-only form or field, the setDisabled(false) method has no effect.

claims.claim: $pages.user.signOut signs out the currently signed-in user.
claims.quote: signOut | Signs out the currently signed-in user.

claims.claim: The client API user reference documents no method for configuring accepted identity providers.

claims.claim: $pages.ajax.request automatically adds the CSRF token to every request.
claims.quote: The token is retrieved when it's first needed, cached in memory, and added to the header of every request. You don't need to retrieve or pass the token.

claims.claim: Ajax requests include the visitor's session cookie.
claims.quote: Credentials: The session cookie is included with every request.

claims.where: Governance guidance: At rollout; Governance controls
claims.claim: The checklist's cloud-flow registration and web-role control has a corresponding controls-table row.
claims.quote: Confirm that any cloud flow a script triggers is registered with the site and secured with a web role, as the cloud flow integration page requires. The table contains table permissions, portals Web API site settings and the undocumented client API switch, but no cloud-flow row.
claims.fix: Add a site-scoped cloud-flow access row with the documented steps: Power Pages > site > + Edit > Set up > Integrations > Cloud flows > + Add cloud flow > flow > Roles > + Add roles > Save, citing https://learn.microsoft.com/power-pages/configure/cloud-flow-integration. Research the automation side before populating it or marking it undocumented.
